name: WPMove Migration Connector Premium
author: xuxu.fr

sections.description:
WPMove Migration Connector moves WordPress posts, pages and custom post types between sites. It has two independent ways to work:

1. File export / import — free, offline, no account required

Straight out of the box, with no sign-up and no API key, the plugin can:

  • Export the posts, pages and custom post types of this site to a portable .json file you download.
  • Import such a file into another WordPress site. Imported items are added as new posts — nothing existing is overwritten or deleted.

This runs entirely on your own server. No external service is contacted, and it is fully functional on its own.

2. Direct site-to-site migration — optional, powered by wpmove.app

If you connect a wpmove.app account, you additionally unlock a live migration that copies content directly between two running sites over their REST APIs, including media (featured images and inline files):

  • Pull mode — install the plugin on the target site to pull content in from a remote source.
  • Push mode — install the plugin on the source site to push content out to a remote target.

This mode is the only practical option when one of the two sites cannot be reached from the internet (localhost, a firewall, a private network). The content travels directly between your two sites; wpmove.app validates your API key, meters your plan’s quota, and records the migration in your history — it never receives your posts or media. This is an optional online service, not a requirement for using the plugin.

Features

  • Free local export of posts, pages and custom post types to a portable file.
  • Optional: export the full taxonomy structure (all terms with descriptions and parent-child hierarchy) so it is recreated correctly on import.
  • Free local import that appends content — no overwrite, no ID conflicts.
  • Optional direct pull/push migration between two live sites, including media and taxonomy terms (requires a wpmove.app account).
  • Resumable direct migrations — an interrupted run skips items already migrated.
  • Cancel a running migration at any time; back button to review results without resetting.

External services

The free file export and import contact no external service whatsoever. The connections below are only made when you use the optional direct site-to-site migration, and only after you enter an API key and start or configure that migration.

1. wpmove.app (the service this plugin pairs with)

The plugin sends requests to your wpmove.app account to validate your API key, report progress after each batch, and close out the migration. The data sent is: your API key, the source and target site URLs, the migration mode, and per-batch counts (number of posts, media and errors). No post content or media files are sent to wpmove.app.

  • Terms of service: https://wpmove.app/terms
  • Privacy policy: https://wpmove.app/privacy-policy

2. The remote WordPress site you configure

The plugin connects to the other WordPress site you specify (the remote source in pull mode, or the remote target in push mode), authenticating with the URL, username and Application Password you provide, to read or write posts and media over that site’s REST API. This is a site you own and control; no third party is involved.
sections.installation:
1. Install and activate the plugin, then open WPMove Migration Connector Premium in the admin menu.
  2. To export: choose Export to a file, pick the post types, and download the file.
  3. To import: choose Import from a file, select the file, and import. Items are added as new posts.
  4. For direct site-to-site migration (optional): on wpmove.app, open My account → Connector, generate an API key, paste it into the API key field and test it. This unlocks pull/push. Then enter the URL, username and Application Password of the remote site and start the migration.
sections.faq:
Do I need a wpmove.app account?

No. The file export and import work fully offline with no account. An account is only needed for the optional direct site-to-site migration (pull/push) between two live sites, which also adds media support.

Does the import overwrite my existing content?

No. The file import is append-only: every item becomes a new post. Nothing on the destination site is overwritten or deleted.

Does the file export include media?

No. The free file export contains posts, pages and custom post types (text, metadata and taxonomy terms). Migrating media files between sites is handled by the optional direct migration with a wpmove.app account.

Does it work between two public, online sites?

Yes. The direct migration works between any two WordPress sites, public or not. If both sites are publicly reachable, the standard tool at wpmove.app is usually the simpler choice; the connector is essential when one of the sites cannot be reached from the internet.

Where does my content go?

Directly between your source and target sites. wpmove.app only receives your API key, the site URLs, and per-batch counts (posts and media migrated) — never the content itself.

What is an Application Password?

A WordPress feature (Users → Profile → Application Passwords) that lets the plugin authenticate to the remote site over the REST API without using your main login password.

Can I resume an interrupted migration?

Yes. The plugin keeps a map of what it has already migrated, so running it again skips items that were already imported.
sections.changelog:
2.6.24

  • New: file export/import carries the site settings too (same rules as the Lite 2.1.14).
  • New: site settings (opt-in, off by default) in pull and push — “Homepage and identity” (homepage, posts page, site icon, logo, translated to the target’s own page and media) and “General settings” (title, tagline, language, timezone, date formats, posts per page). Through the core settings route on both sides; never the site address, the admin email, the theme or plugins. Listed in the pre-migration analysis and logged line by line.
  • Fix: a value the target ignores (a language not installed there) or refuses is reported, never logged as applied.

2.6.23

  • Fix: once a migration had finished, the summary column still said a migration was running (until “Back” was clicked). It now shows nothing to launch, the results being in the Progress card.

2.6.22

  • New: app-style layout, as on wpmove.app — a step sidebar (with your plan and links to your account and help) and a summary column that recaps the mode, the route, the content and the options, with the main action button always in reach.
  • Change: “Import from a file” is now the default mode.
  • Change: mode cards reordered — “Import from a file” before “Export to a file”, then “This site is the target” before “This site is the source”, same order as the Lite.
  • New: refreshed admin screen, aligned with the wpmove.app app — new header, clearer cards, option rows, larger fields and buttons. The WPMove mark replaces the generic menu icon.
  • Fix: the lock icons on the Premium cards are now drawn in CSS instead of an emoji, which some systems rendered as an empty box.
  • Security: comments written by the receiver (/wpmvc/v1/comments) are now filtered like post content when the account cannot post unfiltered HTML (multisite site administrators, DISALLOW_UNFILTERED_HTML). Author name, email and URL are always sanitized.
  • Fix: the file import log now lists the items it skipped, like the Lite.
  • Fix: the source/target order on the direct migration cards (“This site is the source” first).
  • Fix: the ID map table is created without IF NOT EXISTS, which prevented dbDelta() from ever applying a schema change.
  • New: uninstalling the plugin removes the API key, the saved profiles (and their encrypted passwords), any interrupted run, the update cache and the ID map table. The “REST API visibility” choices are kept while the Lite is still installed.

2.6.21

  • New: “Analyze before migrating” button on pull and push. A read-only report of what the migration will do, before you start it: volume per content type, your plan’s limits (contents and media credits), page-builder layouts and whether they will survive, reusable blocks, comments (and whether the target will email its authors), taxonomies and content types the REST API cannot see, and how many items already exist on the target and will be skipped or replaced. With the connector on the other site (2.1.10 or later) the counts and conflicts are exact; without it the report says what it could not check.
  • New: the same pre-import report on the file import screen (see the free plugin 2.1.10), and the /wpmvc/v1/preflight receiver endpoint it relies on.

2.6.20

  • New: the “Taxonomy REST visibility” setting becomes “REST API visibility” and also covers custom post types registered without REST API support — the same opt-in, per type, with the same caveat (an exposed type becomes readable through this site’s public REST API).
  • Fix: an item already opted in disappeared from the list at the next page load (it now had REST support), so it could never be unticked again. Opted-in items stay listed.

2.6.19

  • Fix: in pull mode, the hierarchy of terms of a custom taxonomy whose REST base differs from its name (rest_base) was silently flattened — the remote term index was fetched from /wp/v2/{taxonomy} instead of the declared base. The base is now read from /taxonomies/{taxonomy}, as the push side already did.
  • Change: in push mode, this site’s custom taxonomies no longer need to be REST-exposed here to travel — the source reads its terms locally; only the remote target needs the “Taxonomy REST visibility” opt-in (it creates the terms through its REST API). Built-in taxonomies without a REST route (post formats) stay out.
  • Change: the log line for a taxonomy skipped by a remote target now says it may exist but not be REST-exposed, and points to the setting.

2.6.18

  • New: “Taxonomy REST visibility” setting. A custom taxonomy that a plugin or theme registered without REST API support (show_in_rest) is invisible to pull/push migration — this new opt-in list lets you expose one specifically, on a per-taxonomy basis. Nothing is exposed automatically.

2.6.17

  • Fix: after loading a saved profile, Test and Start were sent without the profile id, so the stored application password could not be used and the remote site answered 401 — it looked as if the password had been erased on every profile switch. The loaded profile now stays attached to the form.
  • Fix: saving a loaded profile as a new one (“Create new”) with the password field left blank produced a profile without any password (the form never redisplays it). The new profile now inherits the password of the profile it was created from.
  • UX: the whole row of a saved profile loads it, not only its name; Rename and Delete keep their own action.

2.6.16

  • New: the receiver endpoint gains POST /wpmvc/v1/comments (announced as comments.write by /ping). When the remote site runs the connector 2.1.7+ / 2.6.16+, push mode writes comments there through wp_insert_comment() instead of the core REST route: no moderation heuristics, no duplicate rejection, no notification email to post authors. The log says which path is in use; without the receiver the core route is kept and the warning stays.
  • Change: pull mode and the receiver now share one insertion routine (WPMVC_Receiver::insert_comment()).

2.6.15

  • Security: reading meta through the receiver endpoint now requires an administrator account too (it returns every meta of a post, protected keys included).
  • Fix: a post status the target does not know is imported as a draft instead of being stored as-is and hidden from every listing.
  • Fix: the log now warns, when comments are migrated in push mode, that the remote site may email each post author once per approved comment (a WordPress setting on that site).

2.6.14

  • Fix: the file export/import dropped every protected meta key (_elementor_data, _wp_page_template, …): a page built with a page builder came back without its layout. Those keys now travel like in direct migrations (ID references still left out, since a file cannot remap them), with the source domain swapped inside them — JSON included.
  • Fix: the file carried the post date in the source site’s local time only; imported on a site in another timezone, a recently published post could turn into a scheduled one. The GMT date is now exported and used on import (older files still import with their local date).

2.6.13

  • Fix: “Skip already migrated posts” did nothing from one run to the next — an item found on the target by slug or title was always rewritten. It is now skipped, unless the run is a sync (a synced item is modified by definition) or “skip” is unchecked.
  • Security: the update package URL carried the account’s API key in a query string (server logs, proxies). The server now hands out a short-lived signed token for that one download; the key stays in the request header everywhere else.
  • Security: writing meta through the connector’s receiver now requires an administrator account. Any account allowed to edit a post could previously write arbitrary meta on it, protected keys included.
  • Security: the remote application password is now encrypted in the migration state stored during a run, like it already was in saved profiles.
  • Fix: a content type whose count could not be read on the remote site was silently treated as empty; the run now stops with the type and the reason.
  • Fix: when the target could not be asked whether a file already exists, the file was re-uploaded (duplicate with a -1 suffix, quota consumed); it is now reported as an error and left alone.
  • Fix: in push mode, a file of this site is read from disk instead of being fetched over HTTP from itself — media no longer fail on a local site with a self-signed certificate or a hostname the server cannot resolve for itself.

2.6.12

  • Fix: the sync-mode re-check of reusable Gutenberg blocks (2.6.11) only found blocks that a post of the same run had already touched — which, by definition, a block edited on its own never is. It now looks the block up on the target by slug/title, like everything else that has to be recognised from one run to the next.
  • Fix: media inside a reusable block are now transferred when the block is re-synced on its own, and media transferred inside any referenced block are now counted against the media quota (they used to travel uncounted).

2.6.11

  • Fix: sync mode (“only migrate content changed since last time”) could miss a reusable Gutenberg block that was edited without touching any post that uses it — the post wouldn’t be picked up again, so the block was never re-synced. A sync run now also re-checks every reusable block modified since the last sync and updates it on the target if it was already migrated before.

2.6.10

  • New: the free file export now bundles any reusable Gutenberg block referenced by the exported items (a wp_block is never itself selectable, but its content can be hidden inside another item’s content). Import recreates those blocks and rewrites the references to point at them, instead of importing content whose blocks point at nothing on the new site.

2.6.9

  • Fix: a reusable Gutenberg block that itself references another reusable block (a chain) now has that inner reference migrated and rewritten too, instead of only the outer one. A reference cycle (two blocks referencing each other) is detected and reported instead of looping.
  • Fix: media (images) inside a migrated reusable block are now transferred like any other inline media, instead of being left pointing at the source.

2.6.8

  • New: a reusable Gutenberg block (<!-- wp:block {"ref":N} /-->) referenced by migrated content is now migrated itself, and the reference is rewritten to point at it on the target — instead of only being flagged in the log (2.6.7). A block that cannot be resolved is still reported rather than left silently broken.

2.6.7

  • New: a reusable Gutenberg block (<!-- wp:block {"ref":N} /-->) referenced by migrated content is now flagged in the migration log. Reusable blocks are not migrated yet (larger feature, tracked separately) — this is visibility only, so the gap is explained in the log instead of showing up unexplained as a missing block in the editor later.

2.6.6

  • New: named, saved migration profiles — set up several pull/push configurations (e.g. one per remote environment), save each under its own name, and switch between them from a “Saved profiles” list instead of overwriting the single stored setup every time.
  • Security fix: the remote application password was sent to the browser and pre-filled into the password field on every page load. It no longer leaves the server; it is now encrypted at rest, and a blank password field falls back to the one already saved on the loaded profile instead of failing.
  • Existing single saved configuration is migrated automatically into a first profile on upgrade — nothing to redo.

2.6.5

  • Fix: a successful key test is now saved immediately, instead of requiring a separate click on “Save”. Testing alone never persisted the key — a page reload silently lost it, and the premium modes had to be unlocked all over again.

2.6.4

  • Fix: a page’s template was never carried over — push and pull now transfer it, falling back gracefully instead of failing the whole page when the target theme does not have that template.
  • Fix: term descriptions are now created and kept in sync, on both new and already-matching terms.
  • Fix: a taxonomy the target site does not have is now reported in the log instead of silently dropping its terms.
  • Fix: the connection test showed a mangled username (e.g. “hellodzgnd-studio” for “hello@dzgnd.studio”) on the source side — it now matches the target side and shows the real login.

2.6.3

  • Fix: another plugin’s admin notice no longer lands in the middle of this page’s header, splitting the title from the text below it.

2.6.2

  • Sync mode no longer goes quiet after a failed run. A migration that ended with errors is no longer used as the “last successful migration” it compares against — what it could not carry over used to fall outside the next run’s window and was never offered again.
  • The log now says so plainly when a run covers everything because the previous one ended with errors.

2.6.1

  • Fix: re-running a migration towards a site that refuses the lookup no longer creates a duplicate. The connector could not tell “this content is not on the destination” from “the destination would not let me look” — so it created instead of updating. It now stops and says so.
  • Fix: content types whose permissions are restricted are no longer written to the wrong address. Their REST route was resolved through a call that silently omits them, so the request went nowhere.
  • New: before a migration starts, the connector checks that the account may actually create each selected content type on the destination, and warns you if not — a custom content type can be off limits even to an administrator.
  • Clearer errors: WordPress uses one and the same sentence for “you may not create as another author” and “you may not create this content type at all”. The second is now spelled out, and the underlying error code appears in the log.
  • The log now names the real content type of each item, and opens with the direction of the migration and the types requested.

2.6.0

  • New: comments now migrate too, with their threads, their dates and their authors’ names. Tick “Import comments” in the options.
  • Comments awaiting moderation come across as well, still awaiting moderation. Spam and trash stay behind.
  • Re-running a migration no longer duplicates comments: one already on the destination is recognised and left alone.
  • Commenters arrive as guests, never attached to an account on the destination — an account id from one site means nothing on another.

2.5.2

  • Fix: adding a content type to a site pair you already sync no longer skips that type’s existing content. Sync mode compares dates, so pages you had never migrated looked “unchanged” and were silently left behind. A migration that widens its scope now runs in full once, and says so in the log.
  • The log also explains the one-off full migration that follows an upgrade from an earlier version.
  • Clearer wording: media files rarely change after upload, so a sync run covering only “Media file” usually carries nothing.

2.5.1

  • Fix: sync mode only filtered the item count, not the items themselves. A sync migration announced “0 items to migrate” and then re-migrated the whole site anyway. Only 2.5.0 was affected.

2.5.0

  • New: sync mode. Tick “Only migrate content changed since the last migration” and a migration carries only what has actually changed since your last successful run between the same two sites — useful for keeping a mirror site up to date without re-sending everything each time.
  • Content deleted on the source is never removed from the destination: sync mode adds and updates, it does not mirror deletions.
  • If there is no previous migration between the two sites, or if the previous one stopped at your plan’s limit, the migration runs in full instead — so content still waiting is never skipped. The log always says which of the two happened, and why.

2.4.8

  • New: relationship, post object, page link and taxonomy fields now migrate. They used to arrive empty, because they hold internal IDs that mean something different on the destination — they are now matched by address rather than by number. A field pointing at content that is not part of the migration is still left empty rather than pointed at the wrong thing, and the log says so.

2.4.7

  • Fix: a migrated page built with Elementor kept loading its images from the original site. Addresses were rewritten in the post content but not inside the builder’s own data, so the pages looked fine until the old site was taken down — exactly when people expect the migration to be finished. Images referenced only from custom fields are now transferred and re-addressed too.

2.4.6

  • Fix: custom post types could fail to migrate. The destination address was guessed by adding an “s” to the type name, which is wrong for many plugins — an Elementor template, for instance, is served at /elementor_library, not /elementor_librarys. The destination is now asked which address it actually exposes.

2.4.5

  • New: page hierarchy is preserved. A child page used to arrive at the top level, detached from its parent.
  • New: menu order is preserved, so manually ordered pages keep their sequence.
  • Fix: a password-protected page lost its password and arrived publicly readable on the destination. The protection is now carried over.
  • Fix: comment and trackback settings were not carried, so the destination applied its own defaults — content with comments deliberately closed could have them reopened.
  • Fix: a child page was duplicated on every migration. It was looked up by its address, which for a nested page includes the parent — so it was never recognised as already migrated.

2.4.4

  • New: the page tree is now preserved. A child page arrived at the root of the site, detached from its parent, and the manual page order was lost as well.
  • New: parent/child category structure is now preserved. A child category used to arrive detached, with its parent missing entirely.
  • Fix: drafts and pending posts were duplicated on every migration. WordPress deliberately gives them no slug — they have no public address — and the slug was the only way to recognise content already migrated. Such content is now matched on its exact title instead.

2.4.3

  • Fix: re-running a migration uploaded every image again instead of reusing the copies already on the destination, filling the media library with -1 and -2 duplicates and consuming media credits each time. Existing files are now recognised across migrations.
  • Fix: with “replace media” enabled, a file referenced more than once (as a featured image and inside a gallery, for instance) was uploaded once per reference, and the featured image could end up pointing at a file that had just been deleted.
  • Fix: posts migrated to a site in a different timezone arrived with a scheduled date in the future, and stayed invisible as a result. Dates now travel in UTC and are converted by the destination.
  • Fix: ACF gallery fields arrived unreadable — the list of images was stored twice-encoded, so the field looked empty in the editor.

2.4.2

  • Improvement: when this site is the source of a direct migration driven from wpmove.app, image and gallery fields now carry enough information for the destination to attach the right file.

2.4.1

  • Fix: the four messages the migration endpoint can return were shown in English regardless of the site language. They are now translatable, and translated in French.

2.4.0

  • New: pull migrations now carry custom fields too, matching what push already did — when the site you pull from also runs this plugin. Elementor layouts, ACF fields and any custom meta come across, images included.
  • Fix: pulling the same content twice re-uploaded its images every time instead of reusing the ones already there, quietly consuming media credits on each run. Files stored at the root of the uploads folder, or filed under a different month on the destination, are now recognised.

2.3.0

  • New: ACF image, file and gallery fields now migrate. Their value is an internal ID that means something different on the destination, so the plugin transfers the file itself and writes the ID it receives back — the field points at the right image, not at whatever happened to share that number. Files already present are reused rather than uploaded twice.

2.2.0

  • New: custom fields that no plugin exposes to the REST API — ACF fields, and any meta added by your theme or a custom plugin — now travel on a push, provided the destination site also runs this plugin. Until now only the fields a plugin had explicitly opened to the API could cross; everything else was dropped without a word. The destination no longer needs the originating plugin installed for the data to arrive.
  • Note: fields whose value is a reference to something else on the source — an ACF image, file, gallery, relationship, post object, taxonomy or user field — are deliberately still skipped. They hold an internal ID that means a different thing on the destination, so copying it would silently attach the wrong file or the wrong post. Resolving them properly is the next step.

2.1.1

  • Fix: on a pull, custom fields containing escaped JSON were silently corrupted — every backslash was stripped on the way in. An Elementor layout arrived with its \u2014 sequences turned into literal u2014, so accented characters and dashes came out mangled in the page. Pushes were never affected.

2.1.0

  • New: direct pull/push migrations now carry post meta (custom fields). Until now the premium connector transferred none at all — less than the wpmove.app service itself. On a pull the target is local, so every field the source exposes is written; on a push the remote site accepts the fields its plugins registered with the REST API. Fields that reference something existing only on the source (edit locks, attachment file paths and sizes, thumbnail IDs) are deliberately never copied — they would break the media that was just transferred correctly.

2.0.9

  • New: after a successful connection test, the plugin now warns you when the remote site does not expose the WPMove meta receiver — meaning custom fields from plugins (Elementor layouts, SEO metadata, ACF) will not be transferred. Until now that loss happened silently, and was only discovered after the migration.

2.0.8

  • Fix: entering this same site’s address as the “remote site” is now refused, both when testing the connection and when starting a migration. Migrating a site onto itself would duplicate every post, page and media file — and “Skip already migrated posts” did not protect against it, since the ID map is empty on a first run. Addresses are compared on site identity, so http/https, a www. prefix, a port or a trailing slash no longer slip through.
  • Fix: a saved but no-longer-valid API key left the premium pull/push modes unlocked and their configuration cards visible. The interface now locks back to file mode when the key check fails, instead of letting you configure a migration the server would refuse.

2.0.7

  • New: the plugin now checks wpmove.app for newer Premium releases and shows a native WordPress “update available” notice on the Plugins page, with a one-click update — no more manually re-downloading from your account page.

2.0.6

  • Fix: the post types list (file export/import and direct migration) can no longer be fully unchecked — at least one type is always kept selected, and the server rejects an empty selection instead of silently falling back to Posts.
  • Fix: testing your API key while “Push” is selected now correctly reports push mode to wpmove.app instead of always reporting pull.
  • Improvement: if one content type fails to load mid-migration while others succeed, it’s now reported in the log instead of being silently dropped.
  • Improvement: reaching your media quota mid-migration now shows a clear note in the log, instead of the media counter just quietly stopping with no explanation.
  • A few remaining hardcoded interface strings are now translatable.

2.0.5

  • Fix: “Media” is no longer offered as a selectable content type in file export/import. That mode never transfers the underlying file (it’s a separate feature from direct pull/push media migration), so selecting it previously created a broken media entry with no file attached on import.
  • Improvement: cancelling a running direct migration (pull/push) now tells wpmove.app the run was cancelled, so it isn’t left open in your migration history. Any media credits already spent during that run are refunded, since a cancelled migration is discarded entirely and fully re-migrated from scratch next time.

2.0.4

  • Fix: a media-heavy batch during direct migration (pull/push) could take longer than the server’s request timeout, silently freezing the progress bar with no error shown. Each request now processes items within a fixed time budget and resumes exactly where it left off on the next request instead of running one long, timeout-prone request per page.
  • Fix: a dropped or failed migration request (network error, server timeout) now shows a clear error message instead of leaving the page looking frozen forever.

2.0.3

  • Fix: selecting a content type other than “Post” in direct migration (pull/push) — Pages or Media File alone — no longer silently migrated actual blog posts instead. Each content type is now read from its own correct REST route.
  • Fix: “Media File” selected on its own now performs a real file transfer (download + attach) instead of creating an empty, file-less media entry. Governed by the existing “Skip already imported media” option (skip vs. replace-in-place), billed against the media quota.
  • Fix: a media-only direct migration is no longer capped by the plan’s per-migration post limit — only the media quota applies.

2.0.2

  • New option to export the full taxonomy structure (all terms with descriptions and parent-child hierarchy). On import, terms are recreated before posts so hierarchy is preserved correctly.

2.0.1

  • Post type selector now lists all public post types registered on the site, not just Posts and Pages.

2.0.0

  • This add-on now bundles both file export/import and direct site-to-site migration (pull/push with media) in a single self-hosted plugin.
  • A separate free Lite plugin (WPMove Migration Connector) handles file export/import for users without a paid account.

1.2.0

  • New: import categories, tags and other taxonomy terms during direct migration (on by default, can be disabled per run).
  • New: Cancel button to stop an in-progress direct migration.
  • New: Back button after a completed migration to return to the config panel without resetting.

1.1.0

  • New: free, offline file export and import of posts, pages and custom post types — no account required. Imports are append-only.
  • The wpmove.app account is now optional and only unlocks direct site-to-site migration (pull/push) and media.

1.0.0

  • Initial release: pull and push migration of posts, pages and media, paired with a wpmove.app account.

short_description: Premium add-on, distributed from wpmove.app. File export/import plus direct site-to-site migration (pull/push) with media, powered by a wpmove.

1. File export / import — free, offline, no account required

Straight out of the box, with no sign-up and no API key, the plugin can:

  • Export the posts, pages and custom post types of this site to a portable .json file you download.
  • Import such a file into another WordPress site. Imported items are added as new posts — nothing existing is overwritten or deleted.

This runs entirely on your own server. No external service is contacted, and it is fully functional on its own.

2. Direct site-to-site migration — optional, powered by wpmove.app

If you connect a wpmove.app account, you additionally unlock a live migration that copies content directly between two running sites over their REST APIs, including media (featured images and inline files):

  • Pull mode — install the plugin on the target site to pull content in from a remote source.
  • Push mode — install the plugin on the source site to push content out to a remote target.

This mode is the only practical option when one of the two sites cannot be reached from the internet (localhost, a firewall, a private network). The content travels directly between your two sites; wpmove.app validates your API key, meters your plan’s quota, and records the migration in your history — it never receives your posts or media. This is an optional online service, not a requirement for using the plugin.

Features

  • Free local export of posts, pages and custom post types to a portable file.
  • Optional: export the full taxonomy structure (all terms with descriptions and parent-child hierarchy) so it is recreated correctly on import.
  • Free local import that appends content — no overwrite, no ID conflicts.
  • Optional direct pull/push migration between two live sites, including media and taxonomy terms (requires a wpmove.app account).
  • Resumable direct migrations — an interrupted run skips items already migrated.
  • Cancel a running migration at any time; back button to review results without resetting.

External services

The free file export and import contact no external service whatsoever. The connections below are only made when you use the optional direct site-to-site migration, and only after you enter an API key and start or configure that migration.

1. wpmove.app (the service this plugin pairs with)

The plugin sends requests to your wpmove.app account to validate your API key, report progress after each batch, and close out the migration. The data sent is: your API key, the source and target site URLs, the migration mode, and per-batch counts (number of posts, media and errors). No post content or media files are sent to wpmove.app.

  • Terms of service: https://wpmove.app/terms
  • Privacy policy: https://wpmove.app/privacy-policy

2. The remote WordPress site you configure

The plugin connects to the other WordPress site you specify (the remote source in pull mode, or the remote target in push mode), authenticating with the URL, username and Application Password you provide, to read or write posts and media over that site’s REST API. This is a site you own and control; no third party is involved.
